summary: Defines DHCP options used by Preboot eXecution Environment and EFI clients to uniquely identify booting machines and their pre-OS environment. This helps the DHCP or PXE boot server return the right bootstrap image. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A computer that just turned on has no software yet. It asks the network who it is and what type it is, so the network can send the right starter program.

questions: how does pxe identify a computer
subtitle: Describing a computer's identity during network boot

tldr.problem: When a computer starts from the network using PXE (Preboot eXecution Environment), it has no operating system yet and needs to ask the server what image to load. The server needs to know what architecture and interface type the client has, and identify the specific machine.
tldr.mechanism: Three new DHCP options tell the boot server the client's system architecture (Intel PC, EFI, etc.), the revision of its network interface driver, and a unique machine identifier (GUID). The server uses these to deliver the correct boot image.
tldr.outcome: Servers can correctly identify booting machines and send them the right operating system or pre-boot application, enabling flexible network boot deployments across multiple hardware types.

today: RFC 4578 is Informational. These DHCP options are widely used in enterprise and cloud infrastructure for network boot and provisioning. They remain the standard way PXE clients identify themselves to boot servers.

sections.title: Network Boot Identification Problem
sections.content:
Preboot eXecution Environment (PXE) allows computers to boot entirely from the network: no hard drive, no local operating system. During startup, the computer's firmware uses DHCP to get network configuration and asks a PXE boot server for a bootstrap image. The server needs to know what image to send.

Early boot servers identified machines by their Ethernet MAC address, but this is insufficient. A single laptop with a docking station might have the same MAC as others in the dock. Conversely, one physical machine might have multiple network interfaces or replacements with different MACs. Additionally, the machine's pre-OS runtime environment (EFI vs. legacy BIOS) affects what code can run. Three new DHCP options solve these problems by letting the client identify itself precisely.
sections.eli5: A computer just turned on. It asks the network 'who should I talk to to get my software?' The network needs to know what kind of computer it is to give it the right answer.

sections.title: The Three New DHCP Options
sections.content:
Option 93: Client System Architecture Type tells the server the machine's pre-boot processor architecture. The option contains one or more 16-bit architecture codes: 0 for Intel x86PC, 2 for EFI Itanium, 6 for EFI IA32, 9 for EFI x86-64, and others. A client that supports multiple boot modes can list several types, and the server picks one that matches an available image.

Option 94: Client Network Interface Identifier specifies the type and revision of the network interface driver the client is running. Currently, type 1 (Universal Network Device Interface, UNDI) is the only supported value. The major and minor revision numbers allow the server to match the driver version. For example, UNDI revision 3.20 is the release version of the 32/64-bit specification with second-generation EFI runtime driver support.

Option 97: Client Machine Identifier carries a unique identifier for the specific machine, most commonly a 16-octet Globally Unique Identifier (GUID). This allows the server to track which machine is booting and retrieve its correct configuration, even if multiple machines have the same architecture and interface type.
sections.eli5: Three labels describe the computer: what kind of processor it has, what version of network driver software, and its unique serial number. The boot server reads these labels to pick the right software to send.

sections.title: Boot Server Usage
sections.content:
A PXE-compliant client must include these three options in all DHCP Discovery and PXE boot server packets. The server inspects them and returns the appropriate bootstrap image or pre-boot application.

The options allow servers to support heterogeneous networks where different machines boot different operating systems or firmware. A server might deliver Windows images to Intel machines, Linux to EFI machines, or diagnostic tools to specific machines identified by GUID.

Options 128 through 135 are also part of the PXE spec, but their format is not defined by RFC 4578; they are reserved for use by downloaded bootstrap programs and are up to individual vendors to define.
sections.eli5: When the computer asks for its software, it includes these labels. The server reads the labels, looks up what software goes with that type and serial number, and sends it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Implications
sections.content:
By specifying incorrect architecture or GUID values, a client could obtain and execute code intended for a different platform, potentially running unauthorized software. Boot servers must validate that the options match expected configurations.

The architecture type and interface version in these options reveal information about the client's hardware and firmware to anyone listening on the network. DHCP traffic is typically broadcast; attackers can monitor it to profile machines on a network. The GUID option reveals a globally unique machine identifier, which could be used to track specific systems across networks if GUIDs are not reissued or randomized periodically.

For these reasons, boot environments should use encrypted channels when possible and implement access controls on PXE boot servers to restrict which machines are allowed to boot which images.
sections.eli5: If the computer lies about what kind it is, it might get software designed for another machine that could cause problems. Also, anyone listening on the network can see these labels and learn about the computers trying to boot.
